doc.title: Sherrie Maricle interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 18, 2001 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Stanley Kay's idea for Diva and the first band's egos
summary: Stanley Kay asked if she knew women who played as well as she did; she helped form Diva, where no one was unique anymore, and the band has matured since 1992.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: We have had some men play with us. Sometimes, just by the nature — the band is at the highest professional level and there aren’t enough women to fill the chairs sometimes. So it’s not a problem with us. But like there’s always the argument of, “well if you’re all so good why do you have to play with each other?” which is kind of insulting. It’s like well, they why don’t you force — and I don’t agree with the issue of like forcing Wynton— there was a big article in the paper about trying to force Wynton Marsalis to hire women or something. And I don’t necessarily agree with forcing the issue. And I know that a lot of bands operate on, these are the people we like to play with because there’s such a collective art form that you can’t apply the same laws of labor to music and say well this has to be a split, you know three Afro-Americans, three women, two Hispanic. There’s no way. It has to be the people you like to work with and the people you gel with the best in your art or it’s not going to be the same band. But when we formed Diva, it was Stanley Kay’s idea, and I played with him, he managed Maurice and Gregory Hines. And there was a concert with Maurice and I was just hired to play drums. And he liked the way I played and it was fantastic music. And a couple of years later he called me up and said “hey do you know women that play as good as you do?” Which to me was unbelievable because he was Buddy Rich’s manager. And I said yeah. And I thought wow, he was so serious and I could tell there was no B.S. in his tone about trying to form a T&A band or anything. Because so many of the bands were, and I played in one in New York sometimes, like an all-women band, a wedding type band, a club date band, to make money, and I would see myself included, but I would see my friends that were so good, like unbelievable musicians in there on a consistent basis. And I used to feel so bad. Like why does that woman have to wear a mini-dress to play alto saxophone when she is the best, she’s a great, great player and she’s just not getting where she needed to be. Well anyway so that was one of my motivations, listening to Stanley and knowing how serious he was and all his influence and connections in music. And I thought good. Because my dream was to be in Woody Herman’s band. And then that went by the wayside and Woody passed away so a big band and trio are my two favorite kinds of drumming. So I was like yeah I’d love to have anything to do with a big band. And I originally wasn’t the leader but I was in there and helped with the original personnel and got the women together. And it was really interesting because what we were saying prior to this was was I looked at as weird as being the only girl drummer. Well everybody in the band probably had a similar experience of, “there’s that girl that can play.” “There’s that good girl trumpet player.” There is like every single person. So then all of a sudden you’re in Diva and everybody plays really great. So in the first band it was so funny because I think it really knocked out of whack the egos that were like I’m unique, I’m unique, I’m a woman jazz artist, I’m unique. And suddenly nobody’s unique. And they
were all like oh, uh oh, I’m sitting next to like five other people who play just as good as I do who are my same gender. I’m not unique anymore. So it was really, really interesting.

To see what happened in the band and everybody like kind of fighting for their solos and their space and everything. The band now is not, since 1992, is not like that anymore. It’s a lot more evolved. And now the purpose of the band, it’s not like a huge, bold, feminist statement, because most of — it is in one respect — but for us it’s great music to play at a really high level and we have, it’s amazing when you have so many fans all over the world literally and it’s funny to go someplace and to hear people like screaming stuff from your CDs and I mean they just really love the band and they love the music, and they love the way we play it. They can identify like a sound with our band, you know, after a relatively short period of time, you know, seven years basically we’ve been working, seven or eight.
